body_markdown:
Failure-to-deposit penalty
The failure-to-deposit penalty is the IRS penalty on an employer that does not make employment tax deposits on time, in the right amount, or in the right way. It is a percentage of the unpaid deposit, from 2 percent to 15 percent, generally depending on how long the deposit stays unpaid, and the highest tier that applies is the total.
Penalty rates
As of November 2026, the IRS figures the penalty in calendar days from the deposit due date, and sends a notice or letter if you owe it.


Timing of the deposit
Penalty
1 to 5 calendar days late
2 percent of the unpaid deposit
6 to 15 days late
5 percent of the unpaid deposit
More than 15 days late
10 percent of the unpaid deposit
Still unpaid more than 10 calendar days after the date of the first IRS notice or letter, or on the day you get a notice demanding immediate payment
15 percent of the unpaid deposit


The tiers replace each other rather than add. For example, a deposit more than 15 days late is charged 10 percent in total, not the 2, 5 and 10 percent tiers combined.
What counts as a failure to deposit
A 10 percent rate also applies to amounts that should have been deposited but were paid directly to the IRS or with the return, except where the payment-with-return exceptions apply. Under IRS Notice 746, that rate also applies to amounts that had to be deposited electronically but were not.


The IRS may also assess an “averaged” penalty of 2 to 10 percent when the actual dates of the tax liabilities cannot be accurately determined. That can happen when liability was $2,500 or more and a monthly depositor did not complete the liability line correctly or a semiweekly depositor did not file Schedule B correctly.
When the penalty can be reduced or removed
Publication 15 says the penalty does not apply to a failure due to reasonable cause and not willful neglect. The IRS decides reasonable cause case by case, asking whether you used ordinary care and prudence and were still unable to comply on time. Reliance on a tax professional, lack of knowledge, mistakes and lack of funds alone generally do not qualify.


The IRS is replacing First Time Abate (FTA) with the Automatic Exemption from Penalty (AEP). As of November 2026, the IRS says AEP is automatic for eligible original returns beginning with tax year 2025 and 2026 quarterly returns, FTA still must be requested from the IRS for some returns processed before AEP starts, and AEP replaces FTA for eligible returns with original due dates on or after January 1, 2027. Both cover the failure-to-deposit penalty.


The IRS reviews your account for a history of timely compliance over the prior three years (or 12 consecutive quarters), and not every business qualifies.
Frequently asked questions
Who is responsible for the penalty when a payroll provider makes the deposits?
The employer generally remains responsible, with an exception for certified professional employer organizations. The IRS says an employer that outsources payroll and related tax duties to a third-party payer will generally remain responsible for those duties, including liability for the taxes. Even when the employer forwards the tax amounts to a third party, the employer remains responsible for deposits and payments, and if the third party fails to make them the IRS may assess penalties and interest on the employer’s account.
How do I ask the IRS to remove a failure-to-deposit penalty?
Start with the instructions in the IRS notice. Call the toll-free number on the notice, or write a signed letter with supporting documents to the address on the notice. If the IRS cannot approve the request over the phone, request relief in writing with Form 843. If you get a penalty notice after you file, reply to the notice with an explanation; the IRS says not to attach an explanation to the return.
Does paying a late deposit stop the penalty from growing?
The IRS says to send a payment or pay the taxes in full to stop future penalties and interest from adding up. An employer that under-deposited can bring deposits up to date through EFTPS. If you cannot pay in full, the IRS says to pay what you can and apply for a payment plan, which “may reduce future penalties.” If you receive a deposit penalty notice, Publication 15 lets you designate how deposits are applied to minimize the penalty if you do so within 90 days of the notice date, following the notice’s instructions.
How is it different from the trust fund recovery penalty?
The failure-to-deposit penalty is a percentage of the unpaid deposit and applies to the employer, while the trust fund recovery penalty equals 100 percent of the unpaid trust fund tax (income tax withheld plus the employee share of Social Security and Medicare tax). The IRS can assess the trust fund recovery penalty personally against a responsible person who willfully fails to collect or pay it over.


Related terms: EFTPS, Form 941, Trust fund recovery penalty.
